 SNAP enrollment in Illinois keeps dropping in wake of 'One Big Beautiful Bill' overhaul
 Participation in the federal food assistance program is at its lowest level since 2009, declining even among children under 18, according to new data from the Illinois Department of Human Services.
 By  
 Elvia Malagón 
 [month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]

 Tucked into the corner of the basement of an Oak Park church, Aida Ayala worked on her laptop as she helped a woman sign up for federal food assistance during Beyond Hunger’s food distribution.
 “Any help will be amazing,” the woman said to Ayala, adding that she was also behind on rent.
 A partition separated Ayala’s workspace from a man demonstrating how to make pumpkin-flavored hummus to a group waiting to pick up groceries. Ayala, a benefit service coordinator for Beyond Hunger, made her way through the list of people trying to navigate the bureaucracy of safety-net programs like the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
 One man wanted to know why he was only receiving $25 in SNAP benefits. Another woman wanted help getting a state identification card.
 Aida Ayala, benefits service coordinator, offers free counseling on SNAP eligibility and access at the Beyond Hunger food pantry location in suburban Oak Park.
 Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times
 Even as food insecurity persists , the number of people receiving food assistance in Illinois continues to decrease months after the state predicted many would lose access due to expanded work rules imposed by H.R.1, more commonly known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” championed by President Donald Trump.
 By September, SNAP enrollment continued to decrease in Illinois to 1.4 million people, the lowest program participation since 2009. That amounts to about a 23% decrease in the number of people getting food assistance compared to last fall. And the future of the program remains uncertain.
 Galvanized by Democrats gaining the majority in Congress, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker issued a list of policy recommendations for federal lawmakers. Repealing SNAP eligibility restrictions and changing the state’s financial burden to administer the program were among Pritzker’s top policy recommendations. At the same time, the Trump administration is proposing another change to SNAP that could further shrink eligibility, the New York Times reported .
 In Cook County, advocates are working to pinpoint what exactly is driving the enrollment decrease. Beyond adults expected to meet the expanded work requirements, participation in Cook County has also fallen among children and those 60 years and older compared from this summer to the fall, according to data from the state.
 Yet, residents are still seeking out the program. In fact, the state received the most SNAP applications from Cook County residents in August and September compared to monthly data from the past two years, according to data from the Illinois Department of Human Services.
 Margarita Muñoz, 56, of Cicero, was among those who applied for SNAP this year. She started receiving benefits in August but it was terminated by the next month for reasons she says are unclear.
 Muñoz found the online application intimidating, but after completing a recent internship with Hunger Free America, she applied and got back on SNAP. She and her son, a sophomore at DePaul University, receive $25 a month in food assistance.
 “Well, $25 is better than nothing,” Muñoz said.
 Confusion leads to terminations 
Earlier this year, Gwynne Kizer Mashon, associate director for the public benefits practice at Legal Aid Chicago, said lawyers got wind that a group of SNAP recipients living in a senior building planned to pull themselves voluntarily from the program because of the H.R. 1 rules. The group, which provides free legal aid, sent a paralegal to reassure the seniors living there that they could keep their benefits.
 “We knew by the definition of them living there, they were exempt,” Kizer Mashon said, referencing the type of building where the seniors lived. “...They were going to proactively stop their SNAP benefits because they were so scared that if they kept their SNAP, that it would interfere with their social security benefits.”
 It’s that type of confusion that could be driving some of the decline in enrollment, Kizer Mashon and other advocates said.
 Congress last year expanded work rules to include 55- to 64-year-olds, veterans and parents whose youngest child is 14 years or older — a change from 18 and older. Individuals have to prove they work or volunteer 80 hours per month to continue getting benefits, but the state has implemented exemptions that would allow people to continue getting food assistance.
 Some exemptions include earning at least $935 per month in gross income, experiencing chronic homelessness or being the main caretaker for an incapacitated or disabled person.
 Lorena Alvarez, community engagement and benefits outreach coordinator, offers handouts to cars in the drive thru line outside the Beyond Hunger food pantry in suburban Oak Park.
 Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times
 Kizer Mashon said they’ve been successful in all but a handful of cases involving people seeking to regain food assistance after they’ve lost it. Legal Aid Chicago has trained pro bono attorneys in Chicago who are also helping people retain their benefits.
 “Most of them qualify for an exemption under Illinois rules, and either they didn’t know that they needed to submit the exemption forms or they submitted them but they got lost or something happened. We don’t know but they weren’t processed,” she said.
 Another source of confusion stems from Illinois SNAP recipients who now have to prove their eligibility every six months instead of once a year, Kizer Mashon said. The notices from the state have caused confusion especially if the person just regained their benefits but remains on the same schedule to prove their eligibility, she said.
 That’s led to instances in which a person gets back on SNAP only to lose it because they were confused about their redetermination date, especially since that process now requires more documentation than before H.R. 1.
 “We think that there are a lot of people who are actually getting back on and then they are losing [SNAP] again because of this end of the certification period,” Kizer Mashon said. “And then they don’t understand what happened so then they just stop. That’s our experience generally with our client community is when things get too confusing, they just stop because they don’t know what else to do.”
 Some additional paperwork includes providing proof of a person’s rent and shelter expenses, which is used to calculate how much in food assistance a household receives, said Autumn Clark, senior manager of public benefits partnerships with the Greater Chicago Food Depository.
 Apart from H.R. 1, advocates say a new federal rule is also causing confusion among potential SNAP enrollees. The Public Charge rule, which went into effect Sept. 18, allows federal immigration officials to deny someone permanent lawful status if they believe the person is likely going to rely on government assistance programs like SNAP.
 Fred Tsao, senior policy counsel at the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, said the rule applies to a small group of people, namely, those who already have green cards and don’t plan on traveling outside the country, or refugees who’ve been granted asylum.
 Tsao said since the rule took effect two months ago, it’s still too early to tell how large of a deterrent effect it’ll have on potential enrollees. But what is clear, he said, is that this most recent iteration of a rule that has been around for over 140 years, is much more confusing.
 “People are worried,” Tsao said. “They don’t know if they are going to apply for SNAP benefits even for a U.S. citizen, spouse,or child. Is that going to count against them?”
 A woman shops for free food during the walk-in client choice market at Beyond Hunger pantry in suburban Oak Park.
 Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times
 ‘Help get something’ 
 Data from the state indicates that people are trying to get food assistance. In August, the state received 40,739 applications for SNAP from Cook County alone, according to the Illinois Department of Human Services. In contrast, the state had received 30,308 applications in August 2025 from Cook County.
 As of September, the state had approved about 166,000 applications from Cook County, compared to the nearly 255,000 applications it approved for all of 2025, according to IDHS. But as of September, the state had also denied about 78,000 applications. The state denied nearly 107,000 applications from the county for all of last year.
 The Greater Chicago Food Depository is among the groups trying to curb the loss of SNAP. In November, the depository added 16 public benefits partners, like Ayala, who help community members keep SNAP benefits. In total, there’s now 40 partners doing this type of work, according to the depository.
 Wanda Taylor, a benefits enrollment specialist at the Greater Chicago Food Depository, jokes that she’s known as the “bag lady” because she travels to community events with paper applications along with her laptop.
 If someone has all their documentation, applying for SNAP could take less than an hour. But the process could take as long as two weeks for those who need time to get their paperwork together because the application adds up to being about 20 pages, she said.
 “People are just really frustrated, confused about those job requirements,” Taylor said. “Do they want to do this for the small amount they may or may not get? … That’s a lot of what I’m hearing.”
 In Springfield, Tsao’s organization is part of a coalition that lobbied to expand a state program that offers food assistance to certain immigrant victims of crime who are seeking asylum or a visa. Pritzker had proposed a $15 million cut to the Victims of Trafficking, Torture, or Other Serious Crimes program.
 And while lawmakers ended up preserving the VTTC program, advocates say the state needs to go further to expand eligibility for lawfully present immigrants, including refugees and their family members, who lost SNAP access this year.
 State Rep. Anna Moeller, D-Elgin, co-sponsored a bill to expand VTTC eligibility during this past spring session, which ended up languishing in House committees. Moeller, who also chairs a Health and Human Services committee, did not commit to bringing the bill back during the fall veto session this month.
 But, she said, everything is on the table.
 “We’re also looking at supporting our food pantries and other ways that people can access food because we know that there are going to be a lot of people who are going to need it,” Moeller said.
 Volunteers distribute free food to cars in the drive thru line outside the Beyond Hunger pantry in suburban Oak Park.
 Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times
 During a recent morning, Muñoz searched for jobs online. She had landed a temporary stint helping others apply for SNAP, but that position was expected to end soon.
 When her two sons were younger, she used SNAP for some years. She later became ineligible after getting a job as a legal secretary. But now, she’s found it difficult to find a permanent role without a college degree. It’s one of the reasons she did the recent internship.
 “I’m hoping everything will tie in and that will get my foot in the door somewhere,” she said.
 Her SNAP benefit doesn’t cover much of her groceries, but she sees it as a way to use $25 of her own money to pay other bills. She was saving the $25 she received for November for a grocery trip closer to the holidays.
 “That will help get something for our Thanksgiving dinner for me and my son,” she said.
 Mawa Iqbal contributing. 
 Various community groups and officials are distributing food ahead of Thanksgiving:
 Metropolitan Family Services, along with Mayor Brandon Johnson and other groups, will distribute turkeys, canned goods and hot meals from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m., Nov. 21, at Riis Park, 6100 W. Fullerton Ave., in Belmont Cragin. 
 Harvest Worship Center Ministries along with other groups will distribute turkey, ham and produce to families from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m., Nov. 21, at 1543 S. Pulaski Rd., in North Lawndale. 
 Ojala Foundation and others will distribute turkeys from 12 p.m. to 4 p.m., Nov. 21, at the Ojala Islamic Center, 1900 S. Oak Park Ave., Berwyn. 
 The Faith Community of St. Sabina Church will distribute turkeys at 12 p.m., Nov. 21, 7800 S. Racine Ave., in Auburn Gresham. For more information, call (773) 483-4300. 
 The Ignatian Mission Center Food Pantry will distribute Thanksgiving groceries from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., Nov. 21, 1735 W Greenleaf Ave., in Rogers Park.
